Indian Geography - Consolidated Revision: Indian Landforms

What this is: a single revision file for India's physiography (landforms), built from the class notes of 1-8 September 2026. For each landform it gives the map first, then the theory, then the important points, then the current affairs (to 15 November 2026). Drainage (rivers) and climate are covered in the other notes and appear here only where they shape a landform.

Source class notes: 1 Sep (location, six divisions) | 2 Sep (Himalaya) | 3 Sep (syntaxes, Purvanchal, IHR, hazards) | 4 Sep (passes, Northern Plains) | 5 Sep (Peninsula, Aravalli, Malwa, Bundelkhand) | 6 Sep (Chota Nagpur, Deccan, Western Ghats) | 7 Sep (Eastern Ghats, Shillong, coasts, A&N) | 8 Sep (Lakshadweep, corals, Thar)

Labels: [Current Affairs] boxes (blue) give dated developments with sources; [Important] boxes (purple) list the points most often tested; [Verification Required] flags figures that sources disagree on; † marks a standard textbook fact or figure not re-checked against a page opened for this file. All maps are schematic: drawn on simplified Natural Earth data, approximate, not to scale and not Survey of India maps.
Contents: 1 Six divisions | 2 Himalaya | 3 Purvanchal and the North-East | 4 Northern Plains | 5 Peninsular Plateau | 6 Thar Desert | 7 Coastal Plains | 8 Islands | 9 Current-affairs table | 10 Mains themes | Key Facts | PYQs

1. The Big Picture: India's Six Physiographic Divisions

1.1 Theory: one story explains all six

India's landforms come from one geological story: an ancient, stable block (the Peninsula, a piece of Gondwana) drifted north and collided with Asia. Each division is a different stage or by-product of that journey.

1. Peninsula = old Gondwana shield (Archaean-Proterozoic rocks, >2,500 Ma in places) → 2. India breaks away and drifts north → 3. passes over the Reunion hotspot: Deccan Traps (~66 Ma) → 4. collides with Eurasia (~50-40 Ma): Himalaya rises → 5. the crust in front of the mountains bends down: a foreland basin filled by Himalayan sediment = Northern Plains → 6. sea-level change, faulting and river deposition shape the coasts; subduction to the east builds the Andaman-Nicobar arc; corals build Lakshadweep
DivisionOrigin and ageRocks / materialDefining features
Northern and north-eastern mountainsYoung fold mountains; India-Eurasia collision from ~50-40 Ma; still risingFolded, thrust-faulted sedimentary and metamorphic rockParallel ranges, deep gorges, glaciers, passes; high seismicity and landslides
Northern PlainsForeland basin filled with alluvium; youngest landformUnconsolidated alluvium, hundreds of metres to several km thick†Flat, fertile; Bhabar, Terai, Bhangar, Khadar; doabs; floods
Peninsular PlateauOldest and most stable block (Gondwana shield)Archaean gneiss, granite, Dharwar schists, Vindhyan sandstone, Gondwana coal, Deccan basaltResidual hills, block mountains, rift valleys (Narmada, Tapi), escarpments (Ghats)
Indian Desert (Thar)Arid region west of the Aravalli; aridity is climaticSand over older rock; dunes, saline lakesBarchans, inland drainage (Luni), playas
Coastal PlainsFaulting (west coast) and river deposition (east coast)Marine and river sedimentWest: narrow, estuaries; East: broad, deltas, lagoons
IslandsA&N: subduction-related uplifted ridge and volcanic arc; Lakshadweep: coral atolls on a submarine ridgeSedimentary/accretionary rock, volcanic rock; coral limestoneBarren Island volcano; atolls, lagoons, reefs
[Important]
  • NCERT uses six divisions; a five-part scheme merges coastal plains and islands.
  • Mainland: 8°4'N to 37°6'N and 68°7'E to 97°25'E; the territorial southern tip is Indira Point, 6°45'N (Great Nicobar).
  • Age order (oldest to youngest): Peninsula (Aravalli = oldest fold mountains) → Deccan Traps (~66 Ma) → Himalaya (~50 Ma onward) → Northern Plains (still forming).
  • Physiography decides climate, drainage, soils, minerals and settlement: e.g. the Himalaya blocks cold Siberian air and traps the monsoon; the Aravalli's SW-NE alignment lets monsoon winds pass Rajasthan without rain.

2. The Himalaya (Northern Mountains)

2.1 Theory: how the Himalaya formed

  1. Tethys Sea: before the collision, the Tethys Ocean lay between India and Eurasia. Its sediments are preserved today in the Tethys Himalaya (marine fossils on high peaks).
  2. Subduction (before ~50 Ma): the oceanic floor in front of India sank beneath Eurasia, producing volcanic and granitic rocks that now form the Trans-Himalaya (Ladakh batholith).
  3. Collision (~50-40 Ma): when continental India reached Eurasia, it could not sink. The crust was folded, faulted and stacked in huge thrust sheets. The join is the Indus-Tsangpo Suture Zone (ITSZ).
  4. Thrusting moved south over time: first the Main Central Thrust (MCT) raised the Great Himalaya; then the Main Boundary Thrust (MBT) raised the Lesser Himalaya; then the Main Frontal Thrust (MFT/HFT) raised the Shiwalik. All branch from one basal fault, the Main Himalayan Thrust (MHT), on which great earthquakes occur (Gorkha, 25 April 2015, Mw 7.8).
  5. Still active: India continues to push north (about 4-5 cm/yr†), so the Himalaya is still rising, very seismic and prone to landslides.

2.2 Longitudinal divisions (south to north)

RangeHeight / width†Key features and examples
Shiwalik (Outer Himalaya)900-1,100 m; 10-50 kmYoungest; unconsolidated sediment from the rising ranges; duns (longitudinal valleys: Dehradun, Kotli, Patli); called Dafla, Miri, Abor, Mishmi hills in Arunachal; Duars in the east are foothill tracts
Lesser Himalaya (Himachal)3,700-4,500 m; ~50 kmPir Panjal (longest), Dhauladhar, Mahabharat; hill stations (Shimla, Mussoorie, Nainital, Darjeeling); Kashmir Valley with Karewas (lake deposits, saffron)
Great Himalaya (Himadri)average ~6,000 mHighest, continuous, granite core, snow-bound; Everest, Kanchenjunga, Nanda Devi, Kamet; glaciers (Gangotri)

2.3 Regional sectors (west to east) and syntaxial bends

  • Punjab / Kashmir-Himachal Himalaya: Indus to Sutlej (~560 km†). Kumaon Himalaya: Sutlej to Kali (~320 km†). Nepal Himalaya: Kali to Tista (~800 km†), the highest. Assam Himalaya: Tista to Dihang (~750 km†).
  • The main arc runs about 2,400 km from the Indus gorge to the Dihang (Siang) gorge, 150-400 km wide.
  • At each end the ranges bend sharply (syntaxial bends): western syntaxis at Nanga Parbat (Indus gorge) and eastern syntaxis at Namcha Barwa (7,782 m, in Tibet, not Arunachal) around which the Yarlung Tsangpo makes its Great Bend.

Rainfall and vegetationLess rain; drier, coniferous; cold desert in LadakhHeavy rain; dense broadleaf forest; biodiversity hotspot
SnowlineLower†Higher (warmer, lower latitude)†
Main hazardAvalanches, cloudbursts, landslides, earthquakesLandslides, floods, GLOFs, earthquakes

2.5 Significance of the Himalaya

  • Climate: blocks cold Siberian winds; forces the monsoon to rise and rain; splits the Subtropical Westerly Jet in winter.
  • Water: part of the Hindu Kush Himalaya (HKH), the "Third Pole" and "Water Tower of Asia"; perennial rivers (Indus, Ganga, Brahmaputra systems).
  • Resources and economy: hydropower, forests, medicinal plants, tourism and pilgrimage (Char Dham, Amarnath).
  • Strategic: natural frontier, but passes have carried trade, invasions and today's border roads.
  • Indian Himalayan Region (IHR): 13 States/UTs = 11 States + 2 UTs (J&K, Ladakh); Assam and West Bengal only through their hill districts.

2.6 Hazards: why the Himalaya is fragile

Natural causes: young, still-rising, fractured rock; steep slopes; active thrusts and earthquakes; glacier retreat leaving moraine-dammed lakes; intense rain and cloudbursts. Human amplifiers: road widening, tunnelling and blasting, hydropower in narrow valleys, deforestation and unregulated construction. Disasters often cascade (rock-ice avalanche → debris flood → dam failure).

EventTypeLesson
Kedarnath, June 2013†Extreme rain + Chorabari lake breach + debris flowPilgrim-route crowding on floodplains
Chamoli, 7 Feb 2021Rock-and-ice avalanche (Ronti peak) → debris flood; destroyed Rishiganga project, hit Tapovan-VishnugadNot a GLOF; hydropower in paraglacial valleys
Joshimath, Jan 2023Land subsidence on old landslide debrisCarrying capacity; drainage; tunnelling concerns
South Lhonak, 3-4 Oct 2023GLOF in North Sikkim; destroyed the 1,200 MW Teesta-III dam at ChungthangMoraine-dammed lakes need early warning
Dharali (Uttarkashi), 5 Aug 2025Debris flow from the Kheer Ganga valleySettlements built on debris fans
[Important]
  • Order south to north: Shiwalik → Himachal → Himadri → Trans-Himalaya; thrusts MFT → MBT → MCT; suture ITSZ.
  • K2 is in the Karakoram (Trans-Himalaya), not the Great Himalaya; Kanchenjunga is on the Sikkim-Nepal border; Namcha Barwa is in Tibet.
  • Duns (longitudinal valleys), Duars (eastern foothill gateways) and Karewas (Kashmir lake deposits) are different things.
  • "La" means pass: "Zoji La Pass" is redundant.
  • Landslides are more frequent in the Himalaya than in the Western Ghats because of young, fractured rock, active seismicity and glacial processes (Mains 2013, 2021).
[Current Affairs] Himalaya
  • New seismic zonation map (BIS IS 1893:2025, November 2025): creates a new highest-risk Zone VI covering the entire Himalayan arc; about 61% of India is now in moderate-to-high hazard zones (Economic Times). [Verification Required: no BIS or PIB primary text was found; check the BIS standard before quoting details.]
  • Glacial lakes: NDMA has assessed 189 high-risk glacial lakes, 56 very high risk. The National GLOF Risk Mitigation Programme (approved 2024, Rs 150 crore) covers Himachal, Uttarakhand, Sikkim and Arunachal; no end-to-end early-warning system had been commissioned by July 2026 (Lok Sabha reply, 23 July 2026; Economic Times). Sikkim is prioritising 16 Category-A lakes after South Lhonak (Sikkim DST).
  • Dharali, 5 August 2025: a debris flow from the Kheer Ganga valley buried parts of Dharali under 12-18 m of debris and partly dammed the Bhagirathi (peer-reviewed study). [Verification Required: casualty figures differ; no single official toll was found.]
  • Kishtwar (Chashoti), 14 August 2025: cloudburst on the Machail Mata yatra route, Paddar (Down To Earth). [Verification Required: death tolls differ between reports.]
  • Himachal: Mandi received 140.7 mm on 1 July 2025, 1,939% above normal (Down To Earth). In the 2026 monsoon, 224 deaths in 55 days (91 rain-related) and losses above Rs 1,121 crore (Indian Express).
  • Joshimath: demolition of 55 unsafe buildings began in July 2026 (Times of India).
  • Tunnels: Sela Tunnel opened 9 March 2024 (13,000 ft, Tezpur-Tawang road; PIB); Sonamarg (Z-Morh) Tunnel opened 13 January 2025 (PIB); Zojila Tunnel (13.153 km) achieved final breakthrough on 9 June 2026, opening expected around February 2028 (Telegraph); Shinku La Tunnel (BRO, Project Yojak, work from July 2024, target 2028). [Verification Required: Shinku La length and cost come from secondary reports only.]
  • Medog (Motuo) dam: China began construction on 19 July 2025 at the Yarlung Tsangpo Great Bend near the eastern syntaxis (planned ~60 GW): a downstream-security and seismic-risk concern for Arunachal and Assam (3 Sep note).

3. Eastern Himalaya, Purvanchal and the North-East

3.1 Theory

  • Beyond the eastern syntaxis (Namcha Barwa), the Himalayan fold belt turns south along the India-Myanmar border. These lower ranges are the Purvanchal: the same mountain system, formed by the same collision, but with much lower relief.
  • They are made mainly of sandstone and shale (sedimentary rock) and are covered with dense forest; ridges run north-south with long parallel valleys.
  • North to south: Patkai Bum (Arunachal-Myanmar) → Naga Hills (Saramati, highest peak of Nagaland) → Manipur Hills (around the Imphal Valley and Loktak Lake) → Mizo (Lushai) Hills (Phawngpui "Blue Mountain", 2,157 m, highest in Mizoram).
  • The Barail Range runs across Assam and separates the Brahmaputra valley from the Barak valley; it is not the India-Myanmar boundary.
  • Not Purvanchal: the Shillong (Meghalaya) Plateau and Karbi Anglong (Mikir) and North Cachar hills are old Peninsular (Gondwana) blocks, separated from the Chota Nagpur-Rajmahal block by the alluvium-filled Malda (Garo-Rajmahal) Gap.

3.2 Shillong Plateau

  • West to east: Garo (Nokrek), Khasi (Shillong, Cherrapunji and Mawsynram), Jaintia hills; Karbi Anglong continues it into Assam.
  • Its steep southern face rises abruptly from the Bangladesh plains, so moist Bay of Bengal winds are forced up: the orographic reason for the world's highest rainfall at Mawsynram-Cherrapunji.
  • Minerals: coal, limestone, uranium (Domiasiat)†; heavy rain on deforested slopes gives badly eroded, laterite-capped surfaces.
[Important]
  • Purvanchal = Himalayan fold belt; Shillong-Karbi Anglong = Peninsular block. A very common trap.
  • Mawsynram and Cherrapunji are in the Khasi Hills; Nokrek (biosphere reserve) is in the Garo Hills.
  • Dampa Tiger Reserve is in Mizoram (Prelims 2015).
  • Assam Himalaya: Tista to Dihang; Siang = Dihang = Tsangpo = Brahmaputra in different stretches.
[Current Affairs] North-East
  • Medog / Motuo hydropower project on the Yarlung Tsangpo Great Bend (construction began 19 July 2025, planned ~60 GW): concerns about flow manipulation, sediment trapping and seismic risk in a high-hazard syntaxis zone. India's response includes the proposed Siang Upper Multipurpose Project as a buffer storage†.
  • Sela Tunnel (9 March 2024) gives all-weather access to Tawang across the Sela Pass (PIB).

4. The Northern Plains

4.1 Theory: formation

  1. As the Indian plate pushed under the Himalaya, its crust bent downward in front of the mountains, like a plank pressed at one end. This created a long depression, the foreland basin (foredeep).
  2. Rivers from the rising Himalaya (and some from the Peninsula) carried enormous loads of sediment into the basin. Over millions of years the alluvium filled it, giving a flat plain about 2,400 km long and 150-300 km wide (Indus-Ganga-Brahmaputra).
  3. Because the mountains are still rising and rivers still flood, the plain is still forming: rivers migrate, braid, meander and change course (avulsion, e.g. the Kosi).

4.2 Belts from the hills to the rivers

BeltMaterialWaterUse / issue
Bhabar (8-16 km)Coarse boulders and pebbles dropped where rivers leave the hillsPorous: streams disappear undergroundPoor farming; key recharge zone
TeraiFine silt and clayStreams re-emerge; marshy, waterloggedForests and wildlife (Dudhwa, Valmiki); much cleared for farming
BhangarOlder alluvium, raised above flood level; kankar (calcium nodules)Deeper water tableMain farmland; less fertile than Khadar
KhadarNew alluvium on active floodplainsRenewed by floods every yearMost fertile; flood-prone; encroachment risk (e.g. Yamuna floodplain)
  • Doab = land between two rivers (Ganga-Yamuna doab); it usually has Bhangar in the middle and Khadar along each river.
  • Floodplain landforms: levees, backswamps, meanders, point bars, oxbow lakes, terraces; in the east, the Ganga-Brahmaputra delta (Sundarbans) and chars (sandbars), and Majuli, a large river island.
  • Sub-regions (west to east): Punjab-Haryana plains (made by the Indus tributaries; doabs), Ganga plains (Rohilkhand, Doab, Awadh, Bihar plains), Bengal delta, Brahmaputra valley (narrow, between the Himalaya and the Shillong-Purvanchal hills).

4.3 Significance and challenges

  • Significance: India's food bowl (Green Revolution from the mid-1960s), densest population, rich groundwater aquifers, inland waterways (NW-1 on the Ganga), cultural heartland.
  • Challenges: groundwater depletion (rice-wheat with free electricity and tubewells in the north-west), arsenic and uranium contamination, waterlogging and salinity, floods and river migration (Kosi), soil fatigue, air pollution (stubble burning, Indo-Gangetic haze), urban floodplain encroachment.
[Important]
  • Order from the hills: Shiwalik → Bhabar → Terai → Bhangar / Khadar.
  • Bhabar is coarse and porous (not fertile silt); Terai is fine and marshy.
  • Khadar does not automatically "become" Bhangar; Bhangar is an older, raised surface left by river incision.
  • The plain is a flexural foreland basin, not one simple syncline.
[Current Affairs] Northern Plains
  • National groundwater assessment 2025: annual recharge 448.52 bcm; stage of extraction 60.63%; 730 of 6,762 units (10.8%) over-exploited (PIB, 15 December 2025).
  • Punjab 2025: extraction at 156.36% of recharge, 111 of 153 blocks over-exploited; uranium above limits in 53% of samples and arsenic in 9.12% (CGWB).
  • Punjab floods 2025 (Sutlej-Beas-Ravi, Bhakra/Pong releases): about 2,050 villages and 20 lakh people affected (see the 14 November note).
  • Mains 2024 asked: "The groundwater potential of the Gangetic valley is on a serious decline. How may it affect food security?" (near-exact).

5. The Peninsular Plateau

5.1 Theory: the oldest block

  • The Peninsula is a fragment of Gondwana: ancient crystalline igneous and metamorphic rock, largely Precambrian, and tectonically stable. Its landscape is the product of long erosion, so it has residual hills, broad shallow valleys and rounded relief.
  • It was shaped by faulting (Narmada-Tapi rift valleys, the Western Ghats escarpment, block mountains such as the Satpura) and by volcanism (Deccan and Rajmahal Traps).
  • Rock ladder (old to young): Archaean gneiss (>2,500 Ma) → Dharwar (3,000-2,500 Ma; gold, iron) → Aravalli Supergroup (2,200-1,800 Ma) → Delhi / Cuddapah → Vindhyan (sandstone, diamonds at Panna) → Gondwana (coal, Damodar) → Rajmahal Traps (~118 Ma, Kerguelen plume) → Deccan Traps (~66 Ma, Reunion plume).
  • General slope is west to east, so most big rivers (Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna, Kaveri) flow to the Bay of Bengal; the Narmada and Tapi flow west in rift valleys and make estuaries.
  • Three divisions: (1) Central Highlands north of the Narmada; (2) Deccan Plateau south of it; (3) Shillong Plateau (detached, section 3). The Narmada-Son lineament separates (1) and (2).

5.2 Aravalli Range

  • Oldest fold mountains in India (Aravalli-Delhi orogeny, Proterozoic), now residual after long erosion. About 670-700 km from Gujarat (near Palanpur) to Delhi (the Delhi Ridge), running SW to NE.
  • Guru Shikhar (1,722 m, Mount Abu) is the highest point; also the highest point between the Himalaya and the Nilgiri.
  • Why Rajasthan is dry: the range lies parallel to the Arabian Sea monsoon branch, so it gives little orographic lift; it acts as a barrier against the eastward spread of the Thar.
  • Water divide: Banas (to the Chambal-Yamuna), Luni (to the Rann), Sabarmati, Sahibi. The Chambal does not rise in the Aravalli (Janapav, near Mhow, Vindhyan).
  • Minerals: Khetri (copper), Zawar (zinc-lead-silver), Makrana (marble), Jhamarkotra (rock phosphate). Mining and NCR construction drive degradation and gaps that let dust and sand reach Delhi.
[Current Affairs] Aravalli: the "100-metre" definition
  • 20 November 2025: the Supreme Court (CJI B.R. Gavai's bench) accepted a uniform definition proposed by a MoEFCC committee: a landform rising 100 m or more above local relief is an Aravalli hill, and two or more such hills within 500 m form a range. It also stopped new mining leases until a landscape-wide sustainable mining plan is prepared (LiveLaw; PIB). The 100 m rule comes from Rajasthan's 2002 use of Richard Murphy's landform classification.
  • Controversy: of 12,081 hills mapped by the Forest Survey of India in the four States, only 1,048 (8.7%) meet the criterion, so most low hills and ridges could lose protection (India Today).
  • 24 December 2025: MoEFCC directed a complete ban on new mining leases across the Aravalli landscape. 29 December 2025: a bench led by CJI Surya Kant put the definition and findings in abeyance (BW Legal World).
  • 25 May 2026: a High-Powered Committee under the ICFRE Director-General was set up. Its interim report (31 August 2026) said a single elevation-based criterion cannot adequately define the Aravallis. On 7 September 2026 the Court refused more time: the final report is due 30 November 2026 and the next hearing is 2 December 2026 (New Indian Express).
  • Aravalli Green Wall Project (MoEFCC, launched 25 March 2023): a 5 km buffer around the range in 29 districts of Delhi, Haryana, Rajasthan and Gujarat (PIB). By January 2026, 6.45 million ha of degraded Aravalli land had been identified and greening started on 2.7 million ha (PIB). Do not confuse it with Africa's Great Green Wall (2007) or China's Three-North Shelterbelt (1978).
  • Exam angle: how a landform is defined decides what is protected: geomorphology (ridge continuity, recharge, wildlife corridors) versus a single height threshold.

5.3 Central Highlands: the Vindhya-Narmada-Satpura structure

  • The Central Highlands lie north of the Narmada, between the Aravalli (west) and the Rajmahal hills (east), and slope north and north-east towards the Ganga plain. Their plateaus (Marwar, Madhya Bharat, Malwa, Bundelkhand, Baghelkhand, Chota Nagpur) are described one by one in 5.5.
  • Vindhya = an escarpment of Vindhyan sandstone facing the Narmada (continued east as the Kaimur), not a fold range.
  • Narmada = a rift valley (graben) between the Vindhya and Satpura; the river follows the fault and flows west to an estuary.
  • Satpura = a block mountain south of the Narmada (Mahadeo hills; Dhupgarh, 1,350 m, highest in MP); continued east by the Maikal range with Amarkantak, the source of the Narmada and Son.

5.4 Deccan Plateau and the Deccan Traps

  • Triangular plateau south of the Narmada, bounded by the Western Ghats (west), Eastern Ghats (east) and Satpura-Maikal-Mahadeo (north). Units: Maharashtra plateau (basalt), Karnataka plateau (Malnad = wet west; Maidan = dry east), Telangana plateau, Rayalaseema, Bastar / Dandakaranya (Bailadila iron ore; Dandakaranya is the wider region).
  • Deccan Traps theory: about 66 Ma, as India drifted over the Reunion hotspot (a mantle plume), huge volumes of basalt lava poured out through fissures in repeated flows. Each flow cooled as a flat sheet, so erosion gives a step-like landscape ("trap" = stair). About 500,000 sq km survives†.
  • Resources (Mains 2022): black (regur) soil for cotton, soybean, jowar and sugarcane; basalt for building and roads; zeolites, agate; bauxite in laterite caps; groundwater only in weathered and jointed zones (hence water stress); scenic and heritage value (Ajanta-Ellora).
  • Not every Deccan unit is basalt: Karnataka, Telangana, Rayalaseema and Bastar are mostly older crystalline rock.

5.5 Each Plateau in Detail

The colour patches on Map 5 show each plateau unit. Read them in three belts: north of the Narmada (Central Highlands), the eastern block (Chota Nagpur to Dandakaranya), and south of the Narmada (Deccan). The Meghalaya (Shillong) Plateau is on Map 3.

North belt (west to east): Marwar upland → Madhya Bharat Pathar → Malwa → Bundelkhand → Baghelkhand → Chota Nagpur | Middle-east: Chhattisgarh basin → Dandakaranya (Bastar) | Deccan (north to south): Maharashtra → Telangana → Karnataka → Rayalaseema → Tamil Nadu uplands | West: Kathiawar | Detached NE: Meghalaya

D. Outliers

PlateauLocationKey points

[Important]
  • Basalt plateaus: Malwa, Maharashtra, Kathiawar (Deccan Traps). Granite-gneiss plateaus: Bundelkhand, Telangana, Karnataka, Chota Nagpur (with Gondwana coal).
  • Malwa slopes north (rivers go to the Yamuna); the Deccan slopes east (rivers go to the Bay of Bengal).
  • Chota Nagpur has radial drainage and is the mineral heartland; Chhattisgarh is a basin, not a plateau.
  • Malnad (west, wet) vs Maidan (east, dry) in Karnataka.
  • Maharashtra and Telangana plateaus are Deccan, not Central Highlands. Dandakaranya is wider than Bastar.
  • Bundelkhand: 7 UP + 6 MP districts; Ken and Betwa are right-bank tributaries of the Yamuna.

5.6 Western Ghats (Sahyadri)

  • Theory: not true mountains but the raised, faulted western edge (escarpment) of the plateau, left when the land to the west subsided into the Arabian Sea after the break-up of Gondwana. Hence a steep western face and a gentle eastern slope, and short, fast west-flowing rivers.
  • About 1,600 km from the Tapi to Kanyakumari across six states (Gujarat, Maharashtra, Goa, Karnataka, Kerala, Tamil Nadu). Heights rise southward: Kalsubai (Maharashtra) → Kudremukh → Doddabetta (2,637 m, Nilgiri) → Anamudi (2,695 m, Anamalai, Kerala: highest in Peninsular India).
  • Palghat (Palakkad) Gap (~30 km wide, ~11°N): the main break; road, rail and moist-wind corridor between Kerala and Tamil Nadu.
  • Significance: orographic rain on the west and a rain shadow on the Deccan; source of the Godavari, Krishna and Kaveri; part of the Western Ghats-Sri Lanka biodiversity hotspot; UNESCO World Heritage (2012, 39 component sites); Nilgiri was India's first biosphere reserve (1986).
  • Governance: Gadgil Committee (2011) proposed treating the whole Ghats as ecologically sensitive (ESZ 1-3, decentralised governance); Kasturirangan Committee (2013) proposed about 37% of the area as an Ecologically Sensitive Area (ESA).
[Current Affairs] Western Ghats
  • Wayanad landslides, 30 July 2024 (Mundakkai-Chooralmala, Meppadi, Vythiri taluk): multiple rain-triggered debris flows; GSI's first report put the source at about 1,544 m and noted the area was only in the moderate zone of the national susceptibility map (GSI). [Verification Required: death tolls range from about 251 to over 400 across sources.]
  • ESA draft notification (seventh issue), 27 July 2026 (S.O. 4106(E)): proposes 56,825.7 sq km as ESA across six States (Karnataka 20,668; Maharashtra 17,340; Kerala 9,993.7; Tamil Nadu 6,914; Goa 1,461; Gujarat 449 sq km). The previous draft had lapsed; drafts lapse after 725 days (Gazette; Hindustan Times).
  • Exam angle: Himalaya vs Western Ghats landslides (Mains 2021): young fractured seismic rock vs old but deeply weathered laterite-soil mantles saturated by intense orographic rain, plus quarrying, plantations and road cuts.

5.7 Eastern Ghats

  • Theory: very old, discontinuous hills, worn down by long erosion and cut through by the Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna and Kaveri, which flow east across them to the Bay of Bengal.
  • North to south: Mahendragiri (Odisha), Jindhagada / Arma Konda (often cited as the highest; published heights vary), Araku valley, Nallamala, Velikonda, Palkonda, Seshachalam (red sanders) in Andhra, Javadi and Shevaroy (Tamil Nadu), B.R. Hills (Karnataka); they meet the Western Ghats in the Nilgiri.
  • Lower, wider-spaced and drier than the Western Ghats; important for tribal livelihoods, bauxite (Odisha-Andhra) and endemic species.
FeatureWestern GhatsEastern Ghats
ContinuityContinuous (main break: Palghat Gap)Discontinuous, cut by large rivers
OriginFaulted escarpment (rift margin)Old eroded hills / residual ranges
HeightHigher (900-1,600 m average†; Anamudi 2,695 m)Lower (~600 m average†)
RiversSource of big east-flowing rivers; short west-flowing riversCrossed by those rivers; few rise here
Rain and vegetationHeavy orographic rain; evergreen forestsLess rain; dry deciduous forests
[Important]
  • Vindhya = escarpment; Satpura = block mountain; Narmada = rift valley (Prelims 2013).
  • Malda Gap separates the Meghalaya Plateau from the Rajmahal-Chota Nagpur block.
  • Anamudi is in Kerala; Doddabetta is in Tamil Nadu.
  • Rajmahal Traps (~118 Ma, Kerguelen) and Deccan Traps (~66 Ma, Reunion) are different events.
  • Granite is intrusive (its volcanic equivalent is rhyolite); India's typical volcanic rock is basalt.
  • Prelims 2026 asked which features belong to the Peninsular block: submergence of the west coast, residual ranges (Velikonda, Mahendragiri) and so on (near-exact).

6. The Thar (Great Indian) Desert

See Map 6 for the desert, the Luni and the saline lakes.

6.1 Theory: why it is a desert

  • Subtropical high pressure: it lies in the belt of sinking, dry air near the Tropic of Cancer.
  • Aravalli alignment: the range runs parallel to the Arabian Sea monsoon branch, so the winds are not forced to rise and rain.
  • Distance and late arrival: it gets the monsoon last and least; rainfall is low (often below 150 mm in the far west†) and highly variable.
  • It was once under the sea (marine fossils near Jaisalmer, Akal Wood Fossil Park†) and later wetter; aridity is relatively recent geologically.

6.2 Features

  • Landforms: barchans (crescent dunes), longitudinal dunes, playas / saline lakes (Sambhar, Didwana, Kuchaman, Sargol, Khatu: Prelims 2021), mushroom rocks.
  • Inland drainage: the Luni (rising near Pushkar-Ajmer) is the only notable river and ends in the Rann of Kachchh; most streams vanish in the sand.
  • Two parts: Marusthali (sandy west) and Bagar (semi-arid strip next to the Aravalli)†.
  • Resources: oil and gas (Barmer), gypsum, lignite, high solar and wind potential; Indira Gandhi Canal irrigation.
[Current Affairs] Thar and Kachchh
  • Thar is greening: a 2025 study found vegetation greenness rose 38% over 2001-2023; about 45% of the rise is linked to higher rainfall and 55% to groundwater pumping for irrigation (Mishra et al., Cell Reports Sustainability, 23 May 2025; DOI). Exam angle: greening through groundwater mining is not sustainable.
  • Khavda renewable energy park (Rann of Kachchh, Gujarat): planned 30 GW over 538 sq km; about 9.4 GW operational by 31 March 2026 (company report). [Verification Required: company source only.]
  • Desertification means land degradation in drylands (UNCCD), not the desert "advancing"; India's target is to restore 26 million ha by 2030.

7. The Coastal Plains

7.1 Theory: why the two coasts differ

  • West coast = submergent (faulted) coast: part of the western margin subsided along faults after the Gondwana break-up, so the plain is narrow (except in Gujarat), and the short, fast rivers from the nearby Ghats form estuaries, not deltas. Drowned valleys make good natural harbours (Mumbai, Mormugao, Kochi). The Malabar coast has kayals (backwaters, e.g. Vembanad).
  • East coast = emergent (depositional) coast: big rivers with large basins carry heavy loads across a gentle slope and build broad plains and deltas (Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna, Kaveri, Ganga-Brahmaputra). The continental shelf is wider; lagoons form behind sandbars (Chilika, Pulicat with its barrier island Sriharikota). Exposed to cyclones and storm surges.
Section (north to south)StretchNote
Kachchh and KathiawarGujaratRann (salt marsh from sea-level fall), Gulf of Kachchh reefs, Gulf of Khambhat
KonkanDaman to GoaNarrow, cliffed; Mumbai
Kanara (Karnataka)Goa to MangaluruNarrow; Netrani island corals
MalabarMangaluru to KanyakumariKayals, lagoons; Kochi
CoromandelTamil Nadu coastKaveri delta; NE monsoon rain
Andhra / Northern CircarsKrishna-Godavari deltas to OdishaKolleru lake between the deltas

[Current Affairs] Coastline
  • Revised coastline: 11,098.81 km (was 7,516.6 km). Re-measured by the National Hydrographic Office and Survey of India using GIS and high-water-line data at 1:250,000 scale instead of the 1970s 1:4,500,000 maps; Ports Ministry circular of 29 April 2025. Gujarat 2,340.62 km (longest State), Andaman & Nicobar 3,083.50 km (longest overall). It will be reviewed every 10 years and does not change CRZ limits. India has 1,298 offshore islands/islets (PIB; Shipping Ministry).
  • The coast did not grow: finer measurement captures more bends, an example of the coastline paradox.
  • Erosion: NCCR found that over 1990-2018, 33.6% of the coast was eroding, 26.9% accreting and 39.6% stable (PIB, December 2023). Mains 2022 GS3 asked about the causes and effects of coastal erosion.

8. The Islands

8.1 Andaman and Nicobar Islands (Bay of Bengal)

  • Theory: the islands are the exposed tops of a submarine ridge formed where the Indian plate subducts beneath the Burma microplate; most are uplifted folded and accretionary sedimentary rocks, with a volcanic arc to the east (Barren Island, India's only confirmed active volcano; Narcondam, dormant†). The same plate boundary produced the 2004 Sumatra-Andaman earthquake (Mw 9.1-9.3) and tsunami.
  • Channels: Coco Channel (North Andaman-Myanmar's Coco Islands), Duncan Passage (South-Little Andaman), Ten Degree Channel (Andaman-Nicobar groups; Prelims 2015), Great Channel (Great Nicobar-Sumatra).
  • Highest point Saddle Peak (737 m, North Andaman); capital Sri Vijaya Puram (formerly Port Blair, renamed 2024); southern tip Indira Point; Great Nicobar Biosphere Reserve (UNESCO MAB 2013). Indigenous communities: Jarawa, Onge, Sentinelese, Shompen, Great Andamanese, Nicobarese.
[Current Affairs] Andaman and Nicobar
  • Great Nicobar Project (transshipment port at Galathea Bay, airport, township, power plant): on 16 February 2026 the NGT declined to interfere, letting the port proceed under the existing environmental clearance and the Island CRZ Notification 2019 (Down To Earth). The project involves felling close to a million trees over about 130 sq km (Frontline).
  • 5 October 2026: the Supreme Court declined the government's plea and asked the Calcutta High Court to fast-track the forest-rights challenge; hearing fixed for 25-26 November 2026 (Hindustan Times).
  • Issues for Mains: strategic location near the Malacca Strait vs leatherback-turtle nesting at Galathea Bay, coral reefs, rainforest, the Shompen (a PVTG), and a very high seismic and tsunami risk zone.
  • Barren Island erupted on 13 and 20 September 2025, the second after a M4.2 earthquake (India Today).

8.2 Lakshadweep (Arabian Sea)

  • Theory: coral atolls built on a submarine ridge (the Chagos-Lakshadweep ridge) as the base subsided and corals kept growing upward (Darwin's subsidence theory).
  • 36 islands, 32 sq km, 12 atolls, 3 reefs, 5 submerged banks; 10 inhabited; capital Kavaratti. Nine Degree Channel separates Minicoy from the rest; Eight Degree Channel separates Minicoy from the Maldives.
  • Corals: polyps are animals living with symbiotic algae (zooxanthellae); bleaching is stress-driven loss of the algae, which can recover if heat stress eases. Indian reef areas: Lakshadweep, A&N, Gulf of Mannar-Palk Bay, Gulf of Kachchh (Prelims 2014), plus patches at Netrani and Malvan.
[Current Affairs] Coral reefs
  • The fourth global bleaching event (2023-25) hit all four Indian reef regions; bleaching reached 84.6% in Lakshadweep; NCSCM has mapped 1,439 sq km of reefs (PIB, 4 December 2024).
  • In 2024 Lakshadweep recorded sea-surface temperature of 32.2°C and heat stress of 9.2 Degree Heating Weeks, the highest on record there (CMFRI).
[Important]
  • A&N = tectonic (uplifted ridge + volcanic arc); Lakshadweep = coral atolls.
  • 8° Channel: Minicoy-Maldives; 9°: Minicoy-rest of Lakshadweep; 10°: Andaman-Nicobar.
  • Barren Island is about 140 km north-east of Sri Vijaya Puram†, not near Great Nicobar.

Key Facts for Prelims

  • Extent: 8°4'N-37°6'N, 68°7'E-97°25'E; Indira Point 6°45'N; Standard Meridian 82°30'E; Tropic of Cancer crosses 8 States.
  • Himalaya: ~2,400 km, Indus gorge to Dihang gorge; Shiwalik → Himachal → Himadri → Trans-Himalaya; MFT, MBT, MCT branch from the MHT; syntaxes at Nanga Parbat and Namcha Barwa (Tibet).
  • Sectors: Punjab (Indus-Sutlej), Kumaon (Sutlej-Kali), Nepal (Kali-Tista), Assam (Tista-Dihang).
  • Purvanchal N to S: Patkai Bum, Naga (Saramati), Manipur, Mizo (Phawngpui 2,157 m). Barail divides Brahmaputra and Barak valleys.
  • Plains: Bhabar 8-16 km (streams sink), Terai (re-emerge), Bhangar (old, kankar), Khadar (new).
  • Aravalli: oldest fold mountains; Guru Shikhar 1,722 m; SW-NE; SC "100 m" definition (Nov 2025) in abeyance; final expert report due 30 Nov 2026.
  • Heights: Anamudi 2,695 m (Kerala), Doddabetta 2,637 m (TN), Dhupgarh 1,350 m (MP), Saddle Peak 737 m (A&N).
  • Plateaus: basalt = Malwa, Maharashtra, Kathiawar; granite-gneiss = Bundelkhand, Telangana, Karnataka, Chota Nagpur; Malwa slopes north; Chota Nagpur radial drainage; Chhattisgarh is a basin.
  • Deccan Traps ~66 Ma (Reunion); Rajmahal Traps ~118 Ma (Kerguelen).
  • Coastline 11,098.81 km (2025 revision); Gujarat longest State; A&N longest overall; 1,298 islands/islets.
  • Channels: 10° Andaman-Nicobar; 9° Minicoy-Lakshadweep; 8° Minicoy-Maldives; Great Channel Nicobar-Sumatra.
  • Lakshadweep: 36 islands, 32 sq km, 10 inhabited, capital Kavaratti; A&N capital Sri Vijaya Puram.
  • Thar saline lakes: Sambhar, Didwana, Kuchaman, Sargol, Khatu; Luni ends in the Rann of Kachchh.

Mains Points

  • Physiography shapes India: climate (Himalayan barrier, orographic rain), drainage (perennial vs seasonal), soils (alluvial, black, laterite), minerals (Peninsula), and settlement (plains density).
  • Himalayan fragility: natural causes + human amplifiers + climate change = more frequent cascading disasters; answer with zonation, carrying capacity, GLOF early warning, Zone VI building codes, Sendai Framework.
  • Peninsular resources: Chota Nagpur minerals, Deccan black soil, Western Ghats water towers; issues: mining, deforestation, Aravalli degradation.
  • Coasts and islands: blue economy and strategic ports (Galathea Bay) vs erosion, cyclones, coral bleaching, tribal rights and seismic risk.
  • Plains: food security vs groundwater collapse in the north-west; arsenic in the middle Ganga; floods in the Kosi-Brahmaputra.

Common Traps / Confusions

  • Namcha Barwa is in Tibet, not Arunachal Pradesh.
  • K2 is in the Karakoram, not the Great Himalaya.
  • Purvanchal is Himalayan; the Shillong Plateau and Karbi Anglong are Peninsular.
  • Chamoli 2021 was a rock-ice avalanche, not a GLOF.
  • Vindhya is an escarpment, not a fold range; the Aravalli runs SW-NE, not N-S.
  • The Chambal rises at Janapav (Vindhyan), not in the Aravalli.
  • Western Ghats are a faulted escarpment, not volcanic mountains (though the north carries basalt).
  • India did not "gain" coast in 2025; the measurement scale changed.
  • Bleached coral is stressed, not necessarily dead; corals are animals.
  • Desertification is land degradation, not desert "advance".
  • Zojila Tunnel and the Sonamarg (Z-Morh) Tunnel are different.
  • The Aravalli "100 m" rule is not current law: it is in abeyance pending the Supreme Court's review.

30-Second Revision

  • One story: Gondwana Peninsula drifts north → Deccan Traps (66 Ma) → collision (50 Ma) builds the Himalaya → foreland basin fills = Northern Plains.
  • Himalaya: 4 parallel ranges, 3 thrusts, 2 syntaxes, 4 sectors; most fragile landform (Zone VI, GLOFs, debris flows).
  • Peninsula: Aravalli (oldest; "100 m" case), Central Highlands, Deccan (basalt, black soil), Western Ghats (escarpment, ESA draft July 2026), Eastern Ghats (broken).
  • Thar: dry by subsidence and the Aravalli's alignment; greening through groundwater.
  • Coasts: west narrow-estuarine, east broad-deltaic; 11,098.81 km.
  • Islands: A&N tectonic (Barren erupted 2025; Great Nicobar case), Lakshadweep coral (84.6% bleaching).

Previous Year Questions (PYQs)

Questions marked "near-exact" were taken from secondary PYQ compilations and not checked against the original UPSC paper.

Prelims

  • 2013: The Narmada flows west while most large peninsular rivers flow east. Why? Answer: it occupies a linear rift valley.
  • 2014: Which of the following have coral reefs? (A&N, Gulf of Kachchh, Gulf of Mannar, Sunderbans). Answer: the first three.
  • 2014: Hill-region pairs: Cardamom Hills, Kaimur Hills, Mahadeo Hills, Mikir Hills (near-exact). Mahadeo-Central India and Mikir-North-East are correct; Cardamom is in the south Western Ghats, Kaimur in the Central Highlands†.
  • 2015: Which pair of islands is separated by the "Ten Degree Channel"? Answer: Andaman and Nicobar.
  • 2017: Statements: the Himalayas are spread over five States only; the Western Ghats over five States only; Pulicat Lake spreads over two States (near-exact). Only the third is correct†.
  • 2018: Barren Island volcano: active; about 140 km east of Great Nicobar; last erupted in 1991 (near-exact). Only "active" is correct: it lies north-east of Sri Vijaya Puram, and it erupted after 1991 (e.g. 2017†, 2025).
  • 2020: Siachen Glacier is situated to the (a) east of Aksai Chin (b) east of Leh (c) north of Gilgit (d) north of Nubra Valley. Answer: (d).
  • 2021: Didwana, Kuchaman, Sargol and Khatu are names of... Answer: saline lakes.
  • 2022: Peak-range pairs: Namcha Barwa-Garhwal Himalaya; Nanda Devi-Kumaon Himalaya; Nokrek-Sikkim Himalaya (near-exact). Only Nanda Devi-Kumaon is correct.
  • 2023: Amarkantak at the Vindhya-Sahyadri confluence; Biligirirangan the easternmost Satpura; Seshachalam the southernmost Western Ghats (near-exact). All three are incorrect†.
  • 2024: Waterfall-region-river: Dhuandhar-Malwa-Narmada; Hundru-Chota Nagpur-Subarnarekha; Gersoppa-Western Ghats-Netravati (near-exact). Only Hundru is correctly matched†: Dhuandhar is near Jabalpur (not Malwa) and Gersoppa (Jog) is on the Sharavathi.
  • 2026: Features of the Peninsular block: submergence of the west coast; residual ranges like the Veliconda and Mahendragiri hills; deep V-shaped valleys (near-exact).

Verification Flags and Notes on Sources

  • Casualty figures for Dharali, Kishtwar and Wayanad differ between sources and are not quoted.
  • The BIS 2025 seismic map (Zone VI) was found only in news reports; check the BIS standard.
  • Shinku La Tunnel length and cost, and Khavda capacity, come from secondary or company sources.
  • Range heights, widths and sector lengths marked † are standard NCERT values not re-checked for this file.
  • Facts carried from the class notes keep the corrections made there (for example Chamoli was not a GLOF; Namcha Barwa is in Tibet).

Pictorial Representations

Included maps (6): six divisions, western and central Himalaya, eastern Himalaya and the North-East, Northern Plains, Peninsular Plateau, coasts, Thar and islands. All are schematic, on simplified Natural Earth data, not to scale and not Survey of India maps.

Included diagrams (2): Himalayan cross-section and plains profile.

[Pictorial Representation Recommended: the Survey of India / NATMO physical map of India for exact relief and boundaries, and the GSI landslide susceptibility map for hazard zones. Suggested sources: Survey of India, GSI Bhukosh.]

Maps and diagrams were checked by script for label overlaps and previewed as images. They were not opened in a desktop browser.
